content: 1. Pertussis, also known as whooping cough, is an acute and prolonged infectious respiratory illness caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis, a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus. 2. Pertussis can lead to significant morbidity in adults and adolescents whose immunity from childhood vaccination or previous infection has waned, particularly if they have not received booster immunization with the Tdap vaccine (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis). 3. In 2004, women aged 15–39 years accounted for 97% of all live births in the United States. 4. Between 2000 and 2006, 103,940 cases of pertussis were reported to the CDC’s National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), with 27% of these cases occurring in individuals aged 15–39 years. 5. Parents with pertussis, including new mothers, are a significant source of pertussis infection in over 25% of cases in early infancy, a period when complications and fatalities are most likely to occur. 6. Infants under 12 months of age accounted for 93% of the 156 pertussis-related deaths reported to the CDC during this period. 7. Decennial booster vaccination with the Td vaccine (tetanus and reduced diphtheria toxoids) has significantly reduced the annual number of tetanus and respiratory diphtheria cases, but pertussis cases remain relatively high, with an average of 14,849 cases annually during the same period. 8. In 2005, two Tdap vaccines were licensed in the United States: Adacel® for individuals aged 11–64 years and Boostrix® for those aged 10–18 years. Both vaccines are approved for single-dose administration. 9. Acellular pertussis vaccines combined with tetanus and diphtheria toxoids are also available in other countries, including many European nations, Canada, and Australia. 10. No vaccine containing acellular pertussis antigens without tetanus and diphtheria toxoids is available in the United States. 11. Vaccinating adults and adolescents with Tdap reduces the burden of pertussis among vaccine recipients and may prevent transmission to infants. 12. 13. ACIP encourages women of childbearing age to receive Tdap during routine health assessments before conception to prevent pertussis morbidity during pregnancy and reduce the risk of transmission to infants. 14. In 2006, ACIP recommended routine administration of Tdap for postpartum women who had not been previously vaccinated with Tdap to provide personal protection and reduce the risk of transmitting pertussis to their infants. 15. The safety and efficacy of Tdap use during pregnancy have not been demonstrated, and Tdap is not recommended for pregnant women in any country. 16. There is no evidence that Tdap administered during pregnancy harms the fetus, increases the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, or negatively impacts an infant’s immune response to later vaccinations. 17. ACIP has suggested that Tdap administered to women in the immediate postpartum period, along with ensuring pertussis vaccination of close contacts, would likely provide protection for both mother and infant. 18. Pertussis is highly infectious, with attack rates among exposed, non-immune household contacts as high as 80–90%. 19. Infants under 6 months of age are at the highest risk for severe pertussis complications, including necrotizing bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and pulmonary hypertension, often requiring hospitalization. 20. The majority of infant pertussis deaths occur among unvaccinated infants, with Hispanic infants and those born prematurely or with low birth weight disproportionately affected. 21. Pertussis is transmitted via large respiratory droplets generated by coughing or sneezing, and untreated patients, particularly infants, can remain infectious for six weeks or longer. 22. Healthcare personnel can transmit pertussis in obstetric and neonatal settings, leading to outbreaks and significant morbidity among hospitalized infants. 23. Early recognition and treatment of pertussis in pregnant and postpartum women, along with prophylaxis for household contacts, are critical to preventing further transmission. 24. Diagnosis of pertussis is complicated by the limitations of current diagnostic tests, with culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) being the only tests accepted for confirming cases for national reporting purposes. 25. Culture is 100% specific for pertussis but has variable sensitivity (30–60%) and requires nasopharyngeal specimens obtained early in the disease course. 26. PCR offers increased sensitivity and faster turnaround times compared to culture but is affected by specimen collection techniques and lacks standardization across laboratories. 27. Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) tests provide rapid results but have lower sensitivity and are subject to interpretation variability. 28. Serologic testing for pertussis requires a substantial change in antibody titers and is typically not useful for clinical diagnosis due to delayed availability of results.
